items.title: Mapping Biome Boundaries From Climate Patterns: A Machine Learning Framework
items.abstract: Aim To develop a climate‐based, probabilistic framework that maps global biomes as climatic domains and explicitly quantifies the spatial distribution and intensity of biome transition zones. Location Global terrestrial biomes. Methods We trained a probabilistic machine‐learning classifier linking biomes to multivariate climate space. We quantified biome ambiguity for each grid cell using Shannon entropy, identifying ecotones as regions where climate supports multiple biome outcomes, that is, high entropy. We applied the framework to present‐day climate and mid‐century climate projections to evaluate potential biome reorganization and ecotone shifts under climate change. Results The model reproduced the broad geographic distribution of major biomes, although spatially blocked validation revealed variation in geographic transferability among biome classes. High‐entropy zones form coherent transition belts that coincide with well‐known ecotones, including forest–savanna boundaries, desert margins, temperate forest–grassland transitions, and the boreal–tundra interface. Biome core regions show low entropy, whereas ecotones exhibit diffuse probability structure and heightened sensitivity to climatic variation. Projections of the model under mid‐century climatic conditions (2041–2060) identify spatially structured patterns of biome transitions, particularly shifts from tundra to boreal forest and from boreal to temperate systems, while also highlighting regions where uncertainty and model disagreement are greatest. Main Conclusions Mapping biomes in climate‐probability space reframes biome boundaries as spatially extended, permeable zones shaped by overlapping climatic regimes. By combining probabilistic classification with entropy‐based uncertainty quantification, our framework complements traditional biome maps by revealing the gradient structure and stability of biome transitions and by identifying where climatic change is most likely to drive ecological reorganization. The resulting transition and uncertainty surfaces offer globally comparable spatial layers for macroecology, biogeography, and evolutionary research, including studies linking ecotones to biodiversity patterns, trait turnover, and lineage diversification.

items.title: Dispersal Limitations Restrict Predicted Climate‐Driven Biodiversity Dynamics Across North America
items.abstract: Aim Species may not fully track shifting climatic conditions when dispersal is limited, yet how species‐specific dispersal constraints scale up to shape biodiversity redistribution across taxa remains unclear. We evaluated how dispersal limitation modifies projected biodiversity dynamics under climate change. Location North America. Time Period Contemporary to late 21st century. Major Taxa Studied Terrestrial vertebrates. Methods We developed species distribution models for 256 terrestrial vertebrate species spanning dispersal rates from 0 to ~100 km/year. We compared climate‐driven projections based on climatic suitability with projections incorporating species‐specific dispersal constraints. We further assessed how dispersal capacity influences habitat accessibility and projected overlap with major land‐cover categories and protected areas. Results Dispersal limitation substantially altered the magnitude and spatial structure of projected biodiversity change. Climate‐driven projections predicted increasing species richness and poleward range expansion, whereas dispersal‐limited projections suppressed leading‐edge expansion, amplified range contraction and generated extensive climatically suitable but inaccessible habitat. These effects intensified under stronger climate forcing and were most pronounced at high latitudes. Species with lower dispersal capacities experienced substantially greater mismatches between climatically suitable and accessible habitat. Dispersal limitation also altered projected landscape overlap: overlap with forests, wetlands, and protected areas increased under climate‐driven projections but declined when dispersal constraints were incorporated, whereas dispersal limitation attenuated projected increases or amplified projected declines in other landscape categories. Main Conclusions Species‐specific dispersal capacity acts as a biological filter on climate tracking, and climate‐driven projections may therefore overestimate species' ability to track environmental change. These species‐level constraints scale up to alter continental biodiversity redistribution and its spatial correspondence with different landscape types. Incorporating dispersal processes is therefore essential for projecting future biodiversity change and informing conservation planning.

items.title: Leveraging Species Associations Patterns of Macroalgae in Wrack to Predict Their Spatial Distribution
items.abstract: Aim Species associations are increasingly recognized as an effective way to improve species distribution model (SDM) predictions by integrating biotic and abiotic information that is difficult to measure in situ. This approach appears promising for monitoring communities where biodiversity and environmental data are sparse or limited. To evaluate its applicability to such communities and to test whether associations estimated in narrow spatial context can capture useful information and be transferred to predict spatial distributions across larger regions, we focused on macroalgal communities in beach wrack. Location France. Methods To estimate the information captured by macroalgae species associations, we assessed the predictive improvement they provide when added to models of increasing complexity using a random forest approach. We also examined how species traits influence association patterns among 58 species observed at 130 sites in Brittany, western France. Finally, we quantified the improvement in predictive performance when applying these associations to species distribution models across 402 sites along the French Atlantic coast. Results We found that species associations both complement and substitute remote sensing and fine‐scale habitat descriptors in predicting individual species distributions. Association patterns were related to certain macroalgae traits (e.g., buoyancy status, initial benthic habitats). They significantly improved large‐scale predictive performance, despite being derived from limited sample sizes and narrow spatial contexts, confirming that such associations capture more than initial or local environmental factors. Main Conclusions Using macroalgal communities in beach wrack, we illustrate that species associations can serve as alternative predictors for communities where biotic and abiotic data are scarce or hard to access. We also highlight their usefulness for predicting at broader spatial scales than those used for their estimation. Leveraging these associations offers promising tools to enhance spatial conservation planning, identify sampling biases and guide efficient surveys (e.g., in exotic or rare species of high conservation concern).
